MESSAGE:
I run deliveries for a small furniture restorer and I've got a few things to sort for tomorrow.

Can you suggest a name for our new delivery van (staff vote, nothing rude)?

Tomorrow the van can't leave the depot before 08:30 and must be back by 12:00. Three drops, each takes 15 minutes to unload. Drop A has a delivery window of 09:00 to 10:00. Drop B is a shop that needs its delivery done before it opens at 09:30. Drop C is an office that won't accept anything before 11:00. Driving times: depot to A 30 min, depot to B 20 min, depot to C 45 min, A to B 25 min, A to C 40 min, B to C 50 min. The driver also needs a 30-minute break somewhere before 12:00. What order should he go in, and what's the timeline?

Could you also rewrite our delivery text so it sounds friendlier than "Driver arriving. Be in."? List three things the driver should check on furniture before handing it over. Should we give customers a paper delivery note or an emailed one? And define "proof of delivery" in a line for our new part-timer. One more thing: we're thinking of texting customers the evening before with a rough arrival time. Could you draft that evening-before text too, keeping it under 160 characters so it goes as a single message?

REQUESTS:
1. Suggest a name for the delivery van
2. Work out the drop order and timeline meeting all time windows, the break and the 12:00 return  KEY: Only feasible order is B -> A -> C. Leave 08:30, arrive B 08:50, unload to 09:05 (done before 09:30); arrive A 09:30, unload to 09:45 (inside 09:00-10:00); arrive C 10:25, wait until 11:00 (take the 30-min break during this wait); unload 11:00-11:15; back at depot 12:00 exactly (zero slack). A-first fails (B reached 09:40, after opening). Must give order B, A, C with a timeline that respects all constraints.
3. Rewrite the delivery text to be friendlier
4. List three furniture checks before handover
5. Recommend paper vs emailed delivery note
6. Define 'proof of delivery' in a line
7. Draft an evening-before arrival text under 160 characters

ANSWER:
## Van name

Since it's going to a staff vote, here's a shortlist to choose from:
- **Dovetail** (the woodworking joint)
- **Patina** (the finish old furniture gets with age)
- **Vin Veneer** (a pun on Vin Diesel)
- **The French Polisher**
- **Chesterfield**

## Tomorrow's route: B → A → C

This is the only order that works:
- **A can't come first.** Its window opens at 09:00, so the earliest finish there is 09:15. The drive from A to B is 25 minutes, so B would be reached at 09:40, after the shop opens.
- **C must be last.** It won't accept anything before 11:00, and A's window closes at 10:00.

| Time | Activity |
|---|---|
| 08:30 | Leave depot |
| 08:50 | Arrive B, unload |
| 09:05 | Leave B (25 minutes before the shop opens) |
| 09:30 | Arrive A, unload (inside the 09:00–10:00 window) |
| 09:45 | Leave A |
| 10:25 | Arrive near C. **30-minute break, 10:25–10:55** |
| 11:00 | Unload at C |
| 11:15 | Leave C |
| 12:00 | Back at depot |

**There is no slack on the return.** C can't start before 11:00, unloading takes 15 minutes, and the drive back takes 45, so arriving at 12:00 is fixed. A delay at C of even five minutes means missing the deadline. It's worth phoning C today to ask them to be ready for the van at 11:00 sharp. Alternatively, check whether the 12:00 return can flex a little.

The rest of the day has some room. The driver can leave A as late as 10:20 and still get to C by 11:00. The break fits with about 5 minutes to spare.

## Friendlier "driver arriving" text

> "Hi [Name], your delivery from [Business] is on its way and should be with you in about [20] minutes. See you soon!"

## Three things to check before handing furniture over

1. **Surfaces and finish.** Look for scratches, dents or scuffs from transit, in good light, with the customer watching.
2. **Joints and moving parts.** Check the piece is stable, doors and drawers open smoothly, and nothing has loosened.
3. **Completeness.** Make sure all parts are there: keys, handles, shelves, glass, fixings. Confirm it's the right item, and that the piece matches the job sheet.

## Paper or emailed delivery note?

**Use email by default and offer paper on request.** Email is easier to keep and to search when a query comes in later. But some customers of a furniture restorer will prefer paper, so keep a few printed copies in the van.

## Proof of delivery, for the part-timer

"Proof of delivery is the record, usually a signature, a photo and the time, showing that the customer received their item in good condition."

## Evening-before text

> "Hi Sam, your furniture from Oakwell Restorations is due tomorrow between 9am and 10am. If that doesn't suit, just reply to this text. Thanks!"

That's **141 characters** with the example name and business, so there are about 19 spare for longer names. Adjust the time window for each customer.

To keep it to one message, make sure the apostrophe in "doesn't" is a plain straight one (') and avoid emoji or curly quotes. Any of those switches the text to a different encoding that limits a single message to 70 characters.
